Connally: she took them off for a while, then unconsciously put them back on.
It happened a third time before she left them off.
Bonnie Ray Williams leaves the sixth floor, which seemed empty to him; the Warren Commission places Oswald there from 11:55 to 12:30.

The chronology argues that in the 10 to 15 minutes left, a lone Oswald would have had to stack some two dozen 50-pound cartons into a nest, assemble the rifle with a dime, and leave just one palm print.
Pauline Sanders, in the second-floor lunchroom until about now, doesn't recall seeing Oswald.
Carolyn Arnold will say she saw him there five minutes later.

Bowers sees a 1961 Chevrolet circle the lot and leave about 12:25, and notices two men behind the fence who stay until after the shots. An older man with "kidney trouble" asks Danny Arce for a restroom in the Depository and later drives off in a black car.
Don Campbell of the Morning News last sees Ruby in the paper's offices about now.
Campbell next sees him at 12:45, leaving a 25-minute gap when some witnesses place Ruby in Dealey Plaza.
Channel 2 reports crowds spilling into the street from Harwood to Ross.
The motorcade pauses at Ervay Street.

Bowers sees a third car, a muddy white Chevrolet Impala with out-of-state plates and one man, probe the lot and pause above the later assassination site. He also sees two men by the fence toward the underpass: one heavyset and middle-aged in a white shirt, one younger in plaid.
Claims (including the Torbitt Document) that H.L. Hunt watched from his office, left Dallas under escort and went to Mexico, or was kept by FBI agents in New York.
Other reports place Hunt in Washington afterwards.
The motorcade passes FBI agent Hosty.
Carolyn Arnold says she glimpsed Oswald on the first floor near the front door.

The pilot car carries Deputy Chief Lumpkin (an Army reserve intelligence officer), Lt. Col. Whitmeyer and advance man Jack Puterbaugh. Its only recorded stop is at Houston and Elm, where Lumpkin briefly talks to the traffic officer; none of the officers there mention it in affidavits.
Channel 2: the rear car reports all is well.

Channel 1 is blocked for at least four minutes by a stuck-open microphone, long attributed to motorcycle officer H.B. McLain; later analysis suggests it may have been elsewhere and that several mikes were keyed. (This recording was the basis of the HSCA acoustics.)
Channel 1 carried routine police business, Channel 2 the visit. County clerks Ronald Fischer and Robert Edwards see a man in an upper Depository window.
They describe him as staring at the knoll area rather than the motorcade, looking uncomfortable, in a light open-necked shirt; one says he had light-colored hair and wasn't Oswald.
Connally recalls dense crowds on Main Street, at least a quarter million along the route, and a good reception everywhere.
The motorcade turns from Main onto Houston, five minutes behind schedule.

Dealey Plaza, named for Morning News founder George Dealey, is a 3-acre park at the city's birthplace, bounded by Houston Street (with the courthouses, jail, Records Building and Dal-Tex Building), with Elm, Main and Commerce converging at the triple underpass and a wooden fence atop the north slope.
The chronology includes occult and Masonic numerology about the plaza (33rd parallel, threes, the Trinity River), offered by a fringe of researchers.
More of the same: James Shelby Downard's ritual reading of the killing and Kennedy heraldry.
And wordplay on "Dealey" and Johnson's middle name.
The motorcade heads straight toward the red-brick Depository before turning left onto Elm.
The chronology notes that a sixth-floor gunman would have had his best shot as the car approached head-on down Houston; it estimates 20,000 open windows and 250,000 spectators along the route.
No precautions are taken for windows, and no report mentions the man holding an open umbrella in the sun.

Only 33 of the building's 69 workers are company employees. The old warehouse is being remodeled; the new passenger elevator stops at the fourth floor and the northwest stairway is closed for repairs, effectively limiting the upper floors to warehouse workers.

Four warehousemen are on the fifth floor at the time of the shots; six had spent the morning laying plywood on the sixth. Warehousemen were paid in cash, and the chronology claims some of the day's time records in the Commission exhibits look fabricated.
Lawson told the HSCA he had nothing to do with choosing the Houston–Elm turn before November 14 and couldn't explain who removed the police homicide car Curry expected.

Sorrels says he glanced at the building from the closed lead car and saw nothing unusual. Some claim Milteer is visible on Houston Street, and that a man in Altgens's photo resembles CIA officer Lucien Conein. Ruby is said to be in the Morning News office nearby, though some witnesses place him in the plaza.

About twenty sheriff's deputies at Main and Houston watch the car pass; of those who gave statements, sixteen later thought the shots came from the knoll area, three had no opinion, and one said the Depository.
Senator Yarborough later describes Johnson listening to a small walkie-talkie held low over the seat.
Manchester portrays Johnson slumped at a low ebb in his career sixty seconds before he becomes President.
Photos show the rear door of Johnson's follow-up car already held open, though some say it was open throughout.
Local reporters had joked all morning about when the shooting would start.

Geneva Hine, alone in the second-floor offices, says the power and phones went dead; the Commission never asked about it. Just after the shots she hears a woman on the phone behind a locked office door.
Bonnie Ray Williams, James Jarman, Harold Norman and Jack Dougherty are on the fifth floor.
Nellie Connally turns and says, "Mr. President, you can't say Dallas doesn't love you."
Kellerman glances at the building without being alerted.

The motorcade turns onto Elm; Zapruder films from the President's right. The Commission computes an average speed of 11.2 mph over the 8.3 seconds before the head shot, assuming 18.3 frames per second. Greer nearly clips a curb on the tight turn, slows, and faces an underpass full of people. David Mantik argues the film lacks the overexposure expected if the camera had been stopped, suggesting frames were removed.
A north wind gust nearly unseats Officer Marrion Baker as he turns onto Houston behind the last press car. Zapruder keeps filming.

Harrison Livingstone describes copies of the Zapruder film going to the FBI, Wade, police, the lab owners, the Secret Service and supposedly H.L. Hunt, and notes a missing processing number (0184) that critics suggest was a Hunt copy.

Homer McMahon of the National Photographic Interpretation Center told the Review Board a Secret Service agent brought the film the weekend after the assassination; from repeated viewing he thought Kennedy was hit six to eight times from three directions, but was told there were three shots from the Depository and to keep the work secret.

French journalist William Reymond says he saw a different version of the film in France. The chronology asks whether a copy was switched for the original, a question it concedes the records cannot settle.
An FBI memo says Kodak in Dallas developed the original and three copies for Zapruder, and the lab asked to copy it.

White House photographer Thomas Atkins films from six cars back with a 16mm camera; his film "The Last Two Days" is called damaging to the lone-gunman finding but was never studied by either federal panel.
In the lead car near the underpass, Sorrels tells Curry five more minutes; Lawson gives the Trade Mart a five-minute warning.
Rose Cheramie, in a Louisiana hospital, says when the motorcade appears on TV that this is when it will happen; she had told an intern a "Jack Rubinstein" was involved.

Justice Department investigator Walter Sheridan is in a Nashville courthouse where Hoffa awaits trial. In the Depository doorway are Frazier, Arce and Lovelady; Roy Truly and O.V. Campbell stand near the oak.
Agent Emory Roberts's shift report records the President arriving at the Trade Mart at 12:35. One writer notes eight agents were assigned to the Trade Mart and none to Dealey Plaza.

The detail's chief, Jerry Behn, stayed in Washington; critics say his stand-in Kellerman was overwhelmed at Parkland, where agents took orders from Emory Roberts, and argue the detail had lost its reflexes.
The chronology contrasts de Gaulle's escorts of up to 47 motorcycles with Kennedy's four at the rear.
The Protective Research Section has 50,000 threat files; it investigated 34 Texans in two years and spent ten minutes on Dallas on November 8.
Army intelligence officer James Powell is in the Dal-Tex Building, which Jim Braden will soon be found leaving.
Deputy Harry Weatherford, a marksman, is on the county jail roof with a rifle.

Altgens, across Elm from the Depository, takes his famous photo about two seconds before the head shot. A man in the doorway resembling Oswald would place Oswald downstairs; the Commission identified him as Billy Lovelady, though the shirt is debated.

Altgens says officers ran up the knoll with guns drawn and that tissue flew from the head toward his side, which critics cite for a frontal shot. The chronology lists security lapses: open car, slow turns, unwatched windows, missing units, unwelded sewer covers.
The chronology says the "barricade" the Commission cited west of the underpass was only a low curb. 178 officers line the route; reserves were told to act only on threats of harm.
Lawson waves at onlookers on the underpass to clear; the officer there doesn't notice. He later asks how 20,000 windows could have been checked.
Rowland notices an officer in front of the Depository. Curry radios the lead car has reached the underpass.
Eight seconds later the dispatcher's time stamp reads 12:30:18. Victoria Adams, on the fourth floor, sees the Kennedys turn toward the building when someone calls out.
Mary Moorman says Jean Hill shouted for the President to look their way as Moorman stepped into the street to take her picture.

In the Zapruder film Moorman appears on the grass, while photo alignment tests suggest she must have been in the street, which alteration theorists cite. Dan Rather, after seeing the film on November 25, describes Kennedy's hand going to his face just before he lurches. Embalmer Thomas Robison described a large hole in the back of the head and small wounds on the right temple and face; some attribute these to pavement debris from a missed shot.
The limousine passes the Stemmons Freeway sign. Groundskeeper Emmett Hudson said the sign was moved soon afterwards and gone by early 1965.
Sylvia Meagher notes no one knows whether it was moved before or after the reenactments, and the Commission never asked.
John Costella argues the sign in the extant film lacks the lens distortion of its surroundings and was inserted; lampposts along the curb were also later moved and shortened.
Hugh Betzner's photo may show another movie camera near Zapruder.
Freshly painted yellow curb stripes appear in the film; some researchers think they were marks for the shooters.
Beverly Oliver, filming near the south curb, later finds yellow paint on her shoes.
A man by the sign opens an umbrella and pumps it as the car passes, then sits beside a dark-complexioned man who appears in photos to hold something like a radio; they leave in different directions.

Penn Jones is tipped that the "Umbrella Man" is insurance salesman Louie Steven Witt, who refuses to talk but says he'll appear before the House committee (he testified in 1978 that it was a protest gesture).

Shots: around Zapruder frame 200 Kennedy's wave freezes and his head turns toward his wife, a reaction the HSCA noted before he goes behind the sign. Hemming claims multiple teams with silencers bought through Mitchell WerBell.
Sheriff Decker and motorcycle officer Stavis Ellis both think they see a bullet hit the pavement; neither is asked by the Warren Commission.
Officer James Chaney tells reporters the first shot missed. James Tague stands near the underpass, about 450 feet from the Depository.
Bowers notices a commotion of some kind behind the fence where the two men stood, which he can't describe.
Mrs. Donald Baker sees a shot strike the pavement near the sign, sparking like a firecracker.
Connally recognizes a rifle shot from over his right shoulder and turns right.
Nellie Connally turns and sees the President clutch his neck and slump without a word; her husband cries out "No, no, no."

James Tague, by the underpass on the Main Street curb, is nicked on the cheek by concrete from a bullet strike more than a block from the car. The Commission didn't question him at first, and he isn't publicly known for seven months.

The chronology says a line from the curb mark back through the President's position points to the Dal-Tex second floor, while the sixth-floor window lies well to the side. Tague later said Hoover didn't want him to exist because he proved there were more shots.
Officer Baker, recovering from the wind gust, hears the shots.
Mrs. Cabell tells the mayor, "Earle, it is a shot."

Kellerman testifies he heard the President say "My God, I'm hit"; no one else in the car recalls it. Kennedy clutches at his throat. The Warren Report said it wasn't necessary to determine which shot hit Connally.
Dr. David Mantik argues witnesses saw Kennedy slump forward twice, and that Jackie lifting him upright, sped up by removed frames, became the "head snap."
